Very well, let us commence with due deliberation; the question before us enquires why parents bid their children to engage in games, and the alternatives presented are thus: mental aptitude, happiness, winning, competitiveness, or entertainment.

One observes, then, that I must first consider with some care the several motives whereby guardians might urge their offspring to play, and it will be prudent to examine each of the enumerated possibilities in turn.

As to mental aptitude (A), it may be plausibly adduced that certain games conduce to the sharpening of cognitive faculties, such as problem solving or the exercise of critical thought; some games do, in truth, afford such benefits, and yet one must pause to ask whether this is the principal inducement which parents, in ordinary practice, propound, and here I confess some uncertainty.

Happiness (B) presents itself as an attractive proposition, for play is delightful and may furnish pleasure to children, and parents, who commonly desire the well being and enjoyment of their young, might therefore recommend games with the hope that pleasure shall ensue; nonetheless the question persists whether this represents the primary motive urged.

With regard to winning (C) and competitiveness (D), these notions seem to relate more narrowly to the character of particular games; where a pastime is of a competitive nature, parents may hope that their children will learn to endure both triumph and defeat, yet it appears to me that the cultivation of a spirit of victory or rivalry is more an incidental consequence than the central reason why parents instruct children to play.

Entertainment (E), on the other hand, presents itself as a straightforward and direct explanation; it would appear quite natural that parents, wishing to employ the leisure of their children to good effect or to occupy them usefully, would recommend games as a source of amusement, and since games are, by their nature, an instrument of entertainment, this seems to be a leading motive.

Yet one must not be precipitous, for it is most curious that some parents employ games with an educational design, which would align with mental aptitude; nevertheless the options are here offered as distinct alternatives, and the question invites us to discern the primary reason for the injunction to play, so that entertainment, being the immediate purpose of the activity, is more general.

I find myself, therefore, oscillating between B and E, and must observe that happiness is an emotional consequence whereas entertainment is the activity itself; if parents bid their children to play, they are, in common parlance, seeking to provide entertainment, which in turn may produce happiness.

In general practice, when parents encourage their offspring to engage in games it is frequently for the sake of amusement and diversion, and thus, though some hesitation existed between joy and entertainment, one concludes that the correct reply is E. So the answer is E.

Let us address this inquiry with due deliberation. The problem is put thus: "It is a teacher's job to help students commit to memory new skills, what is the teacher's main job in the classroom to help students do?" and the alternatives presented are A) make tape, B) memorize, C) never forget, D) concentrate, E) learn.

First, one must endeavour to apprehend with precision what the question truly demands. The preliminary clause asserts that the teacher assists pupils in committing new skills to memory; yet the subsequent interrogative enquires after the teacher's principal duty in the classroom when aiding students to perform some action. Thus the offered alternatives represent several distinct actions, and it becomes necessary to weigh them.

Permit me to analyse the matter methodically. The opening remark concerns the committing of facts or skills to memory, which is plainly allied with the act of memorization; nevertheless the question, as posed, inquires as to the teacher's chief office in this particular context. Among the choices are the plain verb "memorize" (B) and the broader verb "learn" (E).

Observe, if you will, that the teacher's office is described as assisting students to commit items to memory; yet the interrogative asks, "what is the teacher's main job in the classroom to help students do?" Hence, one might at first glance infer that the correct response is not confined to the narrow process of memorizing, for the function of a teacher is ordinarily more comprehensive. Teachers do not, in proper educational philosophy, labour solely to induce rote retention; rather they aspire to shepherd the pupil towards learning in a more expansive sense. Committing to memory constitutes but a portion of the larger enterprise which one dignifies by the name of learning.

Allow me to reexamine the alternatives with care. Option E, "learn," subsumes a variety of cognitive activities, of which memorization is but one constituent. The teacher's duty, broadly speaking, is to facilitate learning, and thus to foster understanding, application, and, indeed, the retention of skills. The sentence which precedes the question might therefore be interpreted as mentioning a particular facet of the teacher's work — the aiding of memory — while the query itself seeks the principal or overarching duty, which would, in my estimation, be to promote learning.

Yet it is prudent to acknowledge the temptation of the contrary reading. If one reads the opening clause as a direct statement of the teacher's work, and then construes the question as asking directly what the teacher is helping the students to do, one could plausibly select B, "memorize," since that word corresponds exactly to the phrase "commit to memory." The juxtaposition of these sentences renders the exercise somewhat ambiguous, and it is most curious that both readings invite consideration.

To resolve this ambiguity, one must adopt the ordinary usage of pedagogic nomenclature. In most accounts of educational duty the primary charge of the teacher is to induce learning; memorization is properly regarded as a technique or instrument towards that end. The initial clause, then, might be a specific illustration rather than the entirety of the teacher's vocation. I observe also that the other options are manifestly less satisfactory: A, to "make tape," is irrelevant; C, "never forget," is ill-formed as an articulated duty; D, "concentrate," denotes a cognitive state of the pupil rather than the teacher's chief function.

Nevertheless the phrasing of the question invites hesitation, for it might be contriving to test whether one is able to distinguish between the narrower process and the broader objective. In such examinations the correct choice is commonly the more comprehensive term when offered, and accordingly one is drawn to prefer E, "learn," over B, "memorize," despite the textual mention of committing to memory.

Hence I am persuaded that the principal duty of the teacher, as evinced by this utterance and by accepted pedagogic doctrine, is to assist students to learn, of which committing matters to memory is but an element; therefore the most accurate selection is E.

Very well; let us examine the inquiry before us with due deliberation: it requests to determine what attribute is common to animals and to humans, and the alternatives furnished are bones, tails, bodies, horns, or a fur coat.

First, it is incumbent upon me to consider each alternative in turn. Commencing with Option A: bones. It is manifest that both man and many animals possess bones; for example, mammals such as dogs, cats, and men exhibit skeletal systems that give form and support to their frames. Yet one must pause and reflect whether there exist animals that lack bones; certain invertebrate creatures spring to mind, and thus a doubt is raised upon the universality of bones among all animals. Nevertheless, humans assuredly possess bones, and the majority of animals commonly conceived do likewise; hence Option A remains a candidate worthy of consideration.

Option B presents tails. It is readily observed that human beings do not possess tails in the ordinary sense; although one may note the presence of a coccyx or tailbone as part of the vertebral column, we do not bear a protruding tail as do dogs or monkeys. Consequently, while some animals display tails, mankind does not; therefore Option B is unlikely to be the correct common attribute.

Option C proposes bodies. Here the matter appears more plain: both humans and animals possess bodies, for every living organism referred to as an animal, and certainly humans among them, are endowed with physical bodies. Even when considered in the broadest and most general view, all animals and human beings are multicellular entities with bodies; thus this alternative commends itself by its generality. Yet one must examine the remaining options before hastily concluding.

Option D suggests horns. It is evident that horns are a feature peculiar to certain beasts—cattle, deer, and some antelopes, for example—and are altogether absent in mankind; hence Option D cannot serve as a universal commonality.

Option E offers a fur coat. Humans do not possess a fur coat in the sense of a dense pelage as bears or cats do; although we have hair upon our bodies, it is not equivalent to a fur coat, and so Option E is likewise excluded.

Having thus compared Options A and C most closely, one observes that the question seeks that which they have in common. If one were to select bones, one would find that whilst humans certainly have bones, not all animals do, for some lack bony skeletons; moreover, bones are merely a constituent part of the larger notion of a body. Therefore, Option C, bodies, being the more general and indisputable attribute shared by both humans and animals, is the preferable and indeed correct choice. Thus the answer is C.

It is consequently most curious that one should pause to consider whether the present question intends a literal geometrical allusion or a figurative application to the character of a document, and one is obliged to suppose, as a provisional hypothesis, that the phrase is employed metaphorically; yet we may note the possibility of a pun, since "obtuse" in geometry contrasts with "acute," and the option E is accordingly labelled "acute angled," which invites the thought that perhaps a non-obtuse thing might be acute.
